newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh apparels lose despite being child free.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh apparels lose despite being child free.

text.p: A U.S. diplomat said on Saturday that Bangladesh's image abroad had improved markedly following elimination of child labour from its apparel industry, but exporters responded by complaining about falling sales and rising costs.

"Unfortunately, we haven't benefited by the way of increased exports. Our cost of production has rather gone up," Nurul Haque Sikder, vice president of the Bangladesh Garments Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) told a reception in honour of the outgoing U.S. ambassador in Dhaka, David N. Merril.
Sikder said apparel exports to the U.S. market dropped by about seven pecent in last 10 months to April compared with the same period of the 1995/96 fiscal year (July-June).
He also expressed concern at the simmering campaign in the United States in favour of improved working environment in third world factories.
"We sense that another danger is coming," a Sikder said.
Bangladesh earned $2.2 billion from exports of textile apparels in the1995/96 fiscal year with nearly 60 percent coming from sales to the U.S. market.
The country is expected to earn $2.6 billion during 1996/97.
By October last year, Bangladesh's garment sector eliminated staff below 14 years of age from their workforces amid intense pressure from the United States.
Around 12,000 retrenched workers are being rehabilitated under a July 1995 agreement between the BGMEA, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and the United Nations Children Fund (UNICEF).
The children have been sent to schools and are being provided with a monthly stipend and vocational training.
The garment manufacturers agreed to the terms after the United States, largest importer of Bangladeshi garments, threatened to stop buying textiles from countries using child workers.
Merril told the reception that Bangladesh's image abroad had markedly improved following the elimination of child labour from its apparel industry.
"Other sectors and other countries are planning to replicate the formula," the U.S. envoy said.
He said Pakistan's soccer ball manufacturing industry, facing international criticism for using child labour, was planning to get rid of under-age workers in a similar way.
